day-07-act-01.title: Closed-book retrieval: values and bindings (Days 04–05)
day-07-act-01.prerequisites: Day 06 completed, including its independent check. If blocked, recover with Day 06 first; for values and bindings, revisit Days 04–05.
day-07-act-01.objective: Recall from memory how repr, type, and bool describe a value, and how rebinding differs from mutation, then confirm with Python on inputs you have not seen before (including empty and Unicode text).
day-07-act-01.assistance_policy_label: Agent-assisted practice: write your own prediction and observed output first; only then may you ask an AI agent to explain or review, and you must record that assistance in your evidence.
day-07-act-01.instructions:
**Spaced review:** Days 04–05 were two to three days ago, so today you retrieve them before rereading anything. Pulling an idea back from memory, then checking it, makes it last longer than rereading notes. Nothing in this activity is new.

1. Close your notes. For each value in the first snippet, write the three columns you expect: repr, type name, and bool. Also predict the last line (len counts Unicode code points, not bytes).
2. Run the snippet and mark every row where your prediction differed.
3. Repeat with the binding snippet: predict both lines, then run it.
4. For each mismatch, write one sentence naming the rule you forgot and the day that teaches it (Day 04 for values, Day 05 for mutation and identity).

```python
def show(value):
    print(repr(value), type(value).__name__, bool(value))
show(0.0)
show("0.0")
show("")
show("猫")
show([""])
show(None)
print(len("猫"), len("café"))
```

```python
a = ["猫"]
b = a
a.append("犬")
print(b, a is b)
c = ["猫"]
d = c
c = c + ["犬"]
print(d, c is d)
```
day-07-act-01.exercise_prompt: Record a prediction table with one row per value (0.0, "0.0", "", "猫", [""], None) and the columns repr / type / bool, plus your prediction for len("猫") and len("café"). Then predict the two lines printed by the binding snippet and explain which name was mutated and which was rebound.
day-07-act-01.hint: The empty string is the only false string; any non-empty string, even "0.0" or a single space, is true. A list that contains an empty string is not empty. append changes the existing list object that both names refer to; c = c + [...] builds a new list and moves only the name c.
day-07-act-01.answer:
Exact output of the first snippet:

```text
0.0 float False
'0.0' str True
'' str False
'猫' str True
[''] list True
None NoneType False
1 4
```

Exact output of the binding snippet:

```text
['猫', '犬'] True
['猫'] False
```

Why: 0.0 and None are false, and "" is the empty string, so it is false; every non-empty string is true, including "0.0". [""] is a list with one element, so it is true. "猫" is one code point and "café" is four. In the binding snippet, a and b name the same list, so append is visible through b and a is b stays True. c + ["犬"] creates a new list; d still names the original ["猫"], so c is d is False.
day-07-act-01.mastery_criterion: Your written predictions exist before execution, cover all six values plus the two len results and both binding lines, and every mismatch has a one-sentence rule and a recovery day (Day 04 or Day 05).

day-07-act-02.title: Retrieval: comparisons and explicit conditions (Days 05–06)
day-07-act-02.prerequisites: Today's activity 1. If comparisons feel unfamiliar, revisit Day 05; for conditions and input normalization, revisit Day 06.
day-07-act-02.objective: Recall the difference between == and is, and rebuild a Day 06-style classifier from memory that handles empty, whitespace-only, decimal, and Unicode-digit input with explicit conditions.
day-07-act-02.assistance_policy_label: Agent-assisted practice: write your own prediction and observed output first; only then may you ask an AI agent to explain or review, and you must record that assistance in your evidence.
day-07-act-02.instructions:
**Spaced review:** this revisits Day 05 (comparisons) and Day 06 (conditions) with new inputs, so you cannot rely on remembered answers.

1. Predict the five booleans printed by the comparison line, then run it.
2. Without looking at Day 06, write label(raw): strip the text; return "missing" if the result is the empty string; return "number " plus the integer value if the stripped text is decimal; otherwise return "text " plus the stripped text. Predict the six printed lines before running your version.
3. Compare your function with the reference below and run both.

```python
print(0 == 0.0, "0" == 0, None is None, [] == [], [] is [])
```

```python
def label(raw):
    text = raw.strip()
    if text == "":
        return "missing"
    if text.isdecimal():
        return "number " + str(int(text))
    return "text " + text
print(label("  猫 "))
print(label(""))
print(label("   "))
print(label("007"))
print(label("-3"))
print(label("٣"))
```

**Optional preview for Day 08 (not assessed, scaffolded):** run the loop below and only observe that its body runs once per character. You will study loops properly tomorrow.

```python

```
day-07-act-02.exercise_prompt: Write your five comparison predictions and your own label(raw), then predict the six outputs for "  猫 ", "", "   ", "007", "-3", and "٣" (ARABIC-INDIC DIGIT THREE). After running, explain the surprising result for "٣".
day-07-act-02.hint: == compares values; is asks whether two names refer to the same object. Each [] creates a new list. Strip first, then test for the empty string: a string of spaces becomes empty after strip(). isdecimal() is True for decimal digits from many scripts, not only 0–9, and int() accepts them.
day-07-act-02.answer:
Comparison output:

```text
True False True True False
```

0 == 0.0 compares numeric values (True); a string never equals an integer (False); None is None is the safe None test (True); two empty lists are equal (True) but are two different objects (False).

label output:

```text
text 猫
missing
missing
number 7
text -3
number 3
```

Trace: "  猫 " strips to "猫", which is not decimal, so "text 猫". "" and "   " both strip to the empty string, so "missing". "007" is decimal and int("007") is 7. "-3" contains a minus sign, so isdecimal() is False and it stays text. "٣" is a Unicode decimal digit, so isdecimal() is True and int("٣") is 3. Preview output: 猫 False, then a True.
day-07-act-02.mastery_criterion: All five comparison predictions and all six label predictions are written before running; your own label(raw) reproduces the reference output exactly; you can explain why "   " is missing and why "٣" is a number.

day-07-act-03.title: Safe Git review: inspect, check, commit, and restore an uncommitted edit
day-07-act-03.prerequisites: Today's activities 1–2; Git installed. If git diff or a small commit feels unfamiliar, revisit Day 04 activity 3 and Day 06 activity 3.
day-07-act-03.objective: Rehearse the Days 04–06 safe-change loop (diff, diff --check, small commit, log) in a disposable repository, and use one new scaffolded command, git restore, to discard an uncommitted edit and verify the result.
day-07-act-03.assistance_policy_label: Agent-assisted practice: write your own prediction and observed output first; only then may you ask an AI agent to explain or review, and you must record that assistance in your evidence.
day-07-act-03.instructions:
**Spaced review:** inspecting a diff before committing was practiced on Days 04 and 06; today you repeat it from memory in a fresh fixture. **New today (scaffolded):** By default, git restore FILE restores a tracked file in the working tree from the index (staging area); it does not change the index or unstage changes. In this fixture the index equals HEAD (the latest commit), so it discards the unstaged edit by restoring that committed version. It cannot undo a commit; Day 09 covers that.

Work only in a new temporary directory, never in the curriculum repository. Before each command, write what you expect it to print (an empty output counts as a prediction). Then run the whole sequence:

```bash
cd "$(mktemp -d)"
git init -q
git config user.name "Learner"
git config user.email "learner@example.invalid"
printf 'label: 猫\n' > notes.txt
git add notes.txt
git commit -q -m "Add notes"
printf 'label: 猫\ncount: 1\n' > notes.txt
git diff --stat
git diff --check
git add notes.txt
git commit -q -m "Add count line"
git log --format=%s
printf 'oops\n' >> notes.txt
git status --short
git restore notes.txt
git status --short
cat notes.txt
```
day-07-act-03.exercise_prompt: Record predictions for the output of git diff --stat, git diff --check, git log --format=%s, and both git status --short commands, then run the sequence and record the actual output. Finally, write the file contents after git restore and explain why the Unicode line "label: 猫" survived.
day-07-act-03.hint: git diff --check prints nothing when there are no whitespace errors. git status --short prints " M notes.txt" (leading space, then M) for an unstaged modification and prints nothing for a clean tree. git restore only touches uncommitted changes, so both commits stay in the log. Never use reset --hard, clean, or force-push here.
day-07-act-03.answer:
Exact output of the full sequence:

```text
 notes.txt | 1 +
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
Add count line
Add notes
 M notes.txt
label: 猫
count: 1
```

Line by line: the diff summary shows one inserted line; git diff --check prints nothing (no whitespace errors); the log lists both commits, newest first; after appending "oops" the short status is " M notes.txt"; git restore copies from the index, which still equals HEAD in this fixture, so the unstaged edit is discarded without changing the index and the second status prints nothing and the file again holds exactly "label: 猫" and "count: 1". The Unicode line survived because it was part of the committed version.
day-07-act-03.mastery_criterion: Predictions are recorded before running; the observed output matches the reference exactly; you can state when git restore is the right tool (uncommitted edit to a tracked file) and that it does not undo commits.

2. From scratch, write describe(raw): return "empty" when the stripped text is empty, "digits" when it is decimal, otherwise "text". Predict and then test it on "", " ", "42", "４２" (full-width digits), and "猫".

day-07-act-04.exercise_prompt: Submit: your three snippet predictions and observed output; your describe(raw) code with five predictions and five observed results; your command list for safe inspection and restoring; and, for any mismatch, the recovery day you will revisit.
day-07-act-04.hint: Use only after an honest attempt: reduce a failing case to one input, compare predicted and observed output, and name the rule involved (empty string, strip, isdecimal, mutation versus rebinding).
day-07-act-04.answer:
Snippet output:

```text
'0' True False
['a', 'é']
['a']
```

A reference describe(raw) and its output:

```python
def describe(raw):
    text = raw.strip()
    if text == "":
        return "empty"
    if text.isdecimal():
        return "digits"
    return "text"
print(describe(""))
print(describe(" "))
print(describe("42"))
print(describe("４２"))
print(describe("猫"))
```

```text
empty
empty
digits
digits
text
```

" " strips to the empty string, so it is empty. Full-width "４２" consists of Unicode decimal digits, so it is "digits". Safe inspection: git status --short, git diff, git diff --check, then git add FILE and git commit only after the diff is understood; discard an uncommitted edit with git restore FILE and confirm that git status --short prints nothing.
